newsitem.title: GERMANY: Muted European reception seen for Intel chip.
newsitem.headline: Muted European reception seen for Intel chip.

text.p: A new microchip about to be unveiled by Intel Corp will bring some dazzling video features to standard desktop computers, but won't do much to jazz up Europe's unsteady retail PC market, analysts said on Monday.

Personal computers using Pentium chips with the new MMX (multimedia extension) technology -- which Intel unveils on Wednesday -- will be able to produce three-dimensional pictures and TV-like video without the extra accessories required today.
But while the MMX chips were expected to crank up the volume for U.S. retailers, the outlook in Europe is clouded by the weak German and French economies, analysts said.
"This technology will give consumers a better product, but I don't know that anyone will be rushing out to buy," said James Bates, an analyst at Context, a PC market research firm in London.

In Germany, Europe's largest PC market, record unemployment and economic uncertainty were likely to keep many home computer users away from new MMX PCs, said Hans Peter Wodniok, a Credit Lyonnais analyst in Frankfurt.

"There is no possibility for double-digit PC growth in Germany this year," he said. "Unemployment is over 10 percent. People aren't sure about their jobs, so at the moment not many can buy a more powerful computer."

Market researcher IDC has predicted European PC growth would reach only about six percent in 1997 -- the lowest level in 10 years. According to Context, European PC sales grew 11.4 percent to 16.5 million computers in 1996, after rising 35 percent in 1995.
In France, where unemployment has surpassed 12 percent, the MMX systems will also have a hard time luring buyers right away, Bates said.
He expected the MMX chips would get a brighter reception in Britain, where a more robust economy produced solid holiday PC sales. Year-end sales in both Germany and France fell below expectations.

In the United States, the Pentium MMX chips were expected to spark a retail boomlet after many consumers postponed holiday purchases in anticipation of the new sound, video and Internet capabilities the technology will offer.
